title: If Christ Is Not Raised
sum: Chapter 15 is the longest sustained argument in the letter, and in many ways its goal. Paul reminds the Corinthians of the good news he gave them: Christ died, was buried, was raised on the third day, and appeared to Peter, the Twelve, more than five hundred, James, all the apostles, and last of all to Paul himself (15:1-11). Some in Corinth say there is no resurrection of the dead. Paul answers that if that is so, Christ is not raised, the preaching is empty and the faith is pointless (15:12-19).

Then he turns it around. Christ has been raised, the firstfruits of the dead, and the rest will follow in order until death, the last enemy, is ended (15:20-28). The chapter ends with the nature of the raised body (15:35-49), the mystery of the last trumpet when the living will be changed (15:50-53), and a taunt to death and a call to steady work (15:54-58).
readings: A defense of a bodily resurrection

On the traditional reading, the Corinthians were drawn to Greek ideas that the soul lives on but the body is useless, and Paul defends the resurrection of the body, with Christ's own rising as proof and pattern. N. T. Wright and many commentators in this line hold that Paul never thinks of the future life as bodiless.

Another reading starts from 4:8, where Paul mocks some Corinthians for thinking they already reign. Perhaps some held that the resurrection had happened already in their spiritual experience (compare 2 Timothy 2:18). Paul then insists that the resurrection is still ahead, tied to Christ's return and the end of death. The two readings are not rivals; most commentators combine them.

views.H: Corinth was a Greek city refounded as a Roman colony, full of mixed cults. Greek tradition offered the soul's immortality (Plato) or no survival at all (Epicureans), and the idea of a dead body being raised was strange to most Gentiles; Athenians mocked Paul for it (Acts 17:32). The Jewish hope of resurrection (Daniel 12:2) was held by the Pharisees but denied by the Sadducees (Acts 23:8). Paul writes from Ephesus, some years after the crucifixion, and the creed of 15:3-5 is older than the letter by a long time.
views.C: Almost no one doubts Paul wrote the chapter. Partition theories, which cut the letter into pieces, mostly leave chapter 15 whole, and some scholars read it as the final proof in a letter-long plea for unity. The verses 3-5 (or 3-7) are widely held to be a pre-Pauline formula. A few scholars call 15:56 or 15:29 later additions; no manuscript omits either. The textual puzzles that change the English are at 15:5, 10, 29, 31, 44, 47, 49, 51, 54 and 55 (see the variant notes). The papyrus P46 (dated between about AD 175 and 225) contains 1 Corinthians, with some lines lost at the foot of each page.
views.L: The chapter is built as a chain of "if ... then": if no resurrection, then Christ not raised (13), then preaching empty (14), faith pointless (17), the dead lost (18). The "But now" of verse 20 breaks the chain. A diatribe objector enters at verse 35, and the answer runs from seed to stars to Adam to the mystery. The Adam and Christ pairs (22, 45-49) hold the whole together. The ending, "your toil is not empty" (58), picks up the word "empty" that rang through the chapter (10, 14).
views.J: Paul argues as a Jew trained among the Pharisees: the resurrection of the dead is the Pharisees' hope (Acts 23:6), the Mishnah later makes it a mark of the faithful (Sanhedrin 10:1), and the shofar is the sign of God's day. His new claim is that the general resurrection has begun in one person. Pinchas Lapide, a Jewish scholar, argued that the resurrection of Jesus was a real event in history, though he did not accept that it made Jesus the Messiah in the Christian sense. Paul's "the law is the power of sin" (56) is read in Jewish scholarship as a statement about the Torah's role, not against it.
views.T: Chrysostom preached on this chapter in his homilies on 1 Corinthians. Irenaeus (Against Heresies 5.9-10) and Tertullian (On the Resurrection of the Flesh) used it against those who denied that the flesh rises. The churches differ on the intermediate state, the nature of the body, baptism for the dead, the Son's subjection and the rapture; the cards below put them side by side.

deep.b:
Paul begins with "I handed on to you what I also received." The wording is compact and rhythmic: four clauses beginning "that" (hoti): Christ died for our sins, was buried, has been raised on the third day, appeared to Cephas and the Twelve. Two of them are "in line with the Scriptures." The Aramaic name Cephas and the phrase "the third day" suggest a Semitic origin, and Paul knew Cephas and James personally from his visit to Jerusalem about three years after his own turning (Galatians 1:18-19). Most scholars of every outlook therefore date the formula within a few years of the crucifixion, which was some years before Paul wrote.

The list of appearances goes beyond the creed: Cephas, the Twelve, five hundred, James, all the apostles, and last of all Paul himself. The Gospels report appearances to Mary Magdalene and the women, which Paul does not list. Why he leaves them out is debated: a list of official witnesses in the style of legal testimony (women did not count as witnesses in some courts), or simply a different tradition.

How scholars explain the appearances. (1) The risen Jesus really appeared in a transformed body (the traditional view; argued by N. T. Wright and Gary Habermas, among others). (2) The disciples had visions, powerful experiences of a living Christ, and not an encounter with a raised body. (3) Jewish scholars: Lapide held that the resurrection of Jesus was a real event in history and a Jewish one, but denied that it made Jesus the Messiah as Christians say. Paul's own claim is that the appearance to him was of the same kind as the others (15:8) and that he is one of the witnesses.
deep.refs: 1 Corinthians 15:3; Galatians 1:18; Luke 24:34; Mark 16:7; Matthew 28:9; John 20:19

deep.b:
Paul never says what the doubters believed, so we reconstruct it from his reply. He attacks a single claim, "there is no resurrection of the dead," with four lines. First, a logical one: no resurrection means no resurrection of Christ (13, 16). Second, what follows for the gospel: the preaching is empty, the apostles are liars, the faith is pointless, sins are not forgiven, and the dead in Christ are lost (14-19). Third, the turn: Christ is raised, and the rising has an order (20-28). Fourth, the practice of the church: baptism for the dead (29), the apostles' danger (30-32), and the slogan of those who give up (32). He ends with a warning against bad company and a call to wake up (33-34).

Paul does not argue from the soul's survival, though he believes in being with Christ after death (Philippians 1:23). His argument is that the whole of human life, including the body, is God's concern and will be redeemed. A modern reader may be tempted to treat the chapter as a proof for the resurrection. Paul's concern is narrower: he assumes the Corinthians believe Christ rose, and shows that denying a general resurrection undoes that.

The questions of 15:35 ("How? With what body?") get a three-part answer. Seeds (36-38): what you sow differs from what grows, and God gives each seed its own body. Many kinds of flesh and glory (39-41): God has made bodies fit for land, air, water and heaven, each with its own glory. Two Adams (42-49): the body is sown in decay, dishonor and weakness, and raised in what cannot decay, in glory and power; sown natural, raised spiritual, as the first man was a living being and the last Adam a life-giving spirit.

The central word is sōma, "body." Readers divide on how "physical" Paul's spiritual body is. A long Christian tradition, with Irenaeus and Tertullian among its early voices, holds that it is the same body, transformed. Wright argues that for a Jew of Paul's time, a spiritual body was a body made new by the Spirit. Dale Martin and Troels Engberg-Pedersen argue that Paul, like Stoics, imagined spirit as a kind of matter, finer than flesh. Robert Gundry argues that sōma means the physical body, even when it is used figuratively. Paul's own point is simpler: continuity and change belong together.

deep.title: Why 'firstfruits'? The day of the sheaf
deep.b:
Paul calls Christ "the firstfruits" (15:20, 23), and he has already called Christ the Passover lamb (5:7). Under Leviticus 23:10-11 the first sheaf of the barley harvest was waved before the LORD "the day after the Sabbath" in Passover week. That the resurrection fell in Passover week, and that "firstfruits" therefore points to the sheaf, is a connection I have not traced to anyone, and I do not claim it. What follows is a narrower question, how exactly the days line up, and the combination below is my own suggestion.

If the Gospel of John is right that Jesus died on 14 Nisan, the Sunday of the rising was 16 Nisan. Josephus (Antiquities 3.248-252) and Philo (Special Laws 2.162) place the offering of the sheaf on 16 Nisan, the second day of unleavened bread, which is the date the Mishnah's side of the dispute below defends. On that count the word "firstfruits" would be an exact match: on the very day the first sheaf was waved, the first of the new humanity was raised. The Boethusians, a Sadducean group, read "the day after the Sabbath" as the Sunday after the weekly Sabbath (Mishnah Menahot 10:3 records the dispute). On their count the sheaf always fell on a Sunday, and the match would hold on the Synoptic Gospels' chronology as well, with the Passover meal on Thursday night. So the answer turns on which calendar the temple kept in the year of the crucifixion, and on how the crucifixion is dated, and neither is settled.

Treat this as an idea, not a finding.

echoes: Genesis 2:7; Genesis 3:19; Genesis 5:3; Psalm 8:6; Psalm 110:1; Isaiah 22:13; Isaiah 25:8; Isaiah 53:5; Hosea 6:2; Hosea 13:14; Daniel 12:2; Leviticus 23:10; Luke 24:34; Luke 24:39; John 12:24; Acts 17:32; Acts 23:8; Romans 5:12; Romans 6:5; Romans 8:11; Romans 8:23; Philippians 3:21; 1 Thessalonians 4:13; 2 Corinthians 5:1; Revelation 20:14

settings.what: The good news and the creed
settings.to: The church at Corinth, including those who said there is no resurrection of the dead
settings.when: from Ephesus, in the spring, before Pentecost (16:8)
settings.why: To remind them of the message they received and on which they stand, and to show that the resurrection is not an extra but part of the first teaching he gave. He lists witnesses who could still be asked (15:6) and puts his own call beside theirs. For the Corinthians, who liked to rank teachers (1:12), it also says that Peter, James and Paul preach the same thing (15:11).
settings.readers: Mixed Jews and Gentiles, mostly Gentile, in a Roman colony of former slaves, merchants and officials, who had been taught about Christ's rising but whose culture found a raised body odd.

settings.what: The answer to those who deny the resurrection
settings.to: The whole church, and the "some" among them who deny it
settings.when: same occasion as 15:1-11: from Ephesus, in the spring, before Pentecost (16:8)
settings.why: To show that denying the resurrection of the dead cancels the resurrection of Christ and with it the gospel, the apostles' honesty, the forgiveness of sins and the hope of the dead in Christ; and then to show what Christ's rising means: the beginning of the end of every power, death included. He appeals to the church's own practice (15:29) and to the apostles' suffering (15:30-32).
views: The deniers followed Greek thought that held the soul immortal and the body a hindrance, or denied life after death altogether.
The deniers thought the resurrection was spiritual and already past, as Hymenaeus and Philetus later did (2 Timothy 2:18).

settings.what: The objector's questions and the seed
settings.to: An imagined objector who asks how the dead are raised and with what body, in a Corinthian church that shared the objector's doubt
settings.when: same occasion as 15:1-11: from Ephesus, in the spring, before Pentecost (16:8)
settings.why: To answer the objection that a raised body is absurd by pointing to what everyone knows: a seed, many kinds of flesh, the sun and stars. The point is that God is the maker of bodies of many kinds, and the next body is as new as a plant is from a seed. The pair of Adams then shows the pattern: from earthly to heavenly.

settings.what: The mystery of the last trumpet and the closing charge
settings.to: The whole church, "we" including Paul and the Corinthians, living and dead
settings.when: same occasion as 15:1-11: from Ephesus, in the spring, before Pentecost (16:8)
settings.why: To say that no one enters God's kingdom as they are, and that both the dead and the living will be changed, at the last trumpet. It ends with thanks and a call to steady work, so that the doctrine becomes a way of living now.

traditions.q: Paul says they are saved "if you hold fast" (15:2). Can a true believer fall away?
views: Perseverance is a gift of God, and "except by special revelation" no one can know for certain that he is among the chosen (Council of Trent, session 6, chapters 12 and 13). Faith is a free gift that can be lost (Catechism 162), and the faithful "hope for the grace of final perseverance" (Catechism 2016).

The OCA adult manual teaches that God works in us only when we cooperate with him (synergeia), and that even after receiving the Holy Spirit "we continue to struggle with 'the old man'." The OCA also teaches that a baptized Christian "can surely fall away," and that "we always have the possibility to repent."
The Augsburg Confession (article 12) condemns those who deny that the justified can lose the Holy Spirit, and teaches that those who fall after baptism can be forgiven when they repent.

True believers "can neither totally nor finally fall away" because God keeps them (Westminster Confession 17.1). Calvin on 15:2 reads "unless in vain" as a warning that the Corinthians would have "needlessly and uselessly professed allegiance to Christ, if they did not hold fast this main doctrine" of the resurrection; he took their quick lapse as a sign that their knowledge had been "loose and floating."

Article 12 of the Articles of Religion says that "after we have received the Holy Ghost, we may depart from grace given, and fall into sin," and that "not every sin willingly committed after justification is the sin against the Holy Ghost, and unpardonable."

The Baptist Faith and Message (2000, article 5) says that all true believers endure to the end, and that those whom God has accepted "will never fall away from the state of grace"; they may fall into sin, but "shall be kept by the power of God through faith unto salvation."

traditions.q: What was 'baptism for the dead', and do any churches practice it?
views: Paul mentions a practice without approving it. The Catholic Church does not baptize the living for the dead, but helps the dead by prayer and above all by the Eucharistic sacrifice (Catechism 1032, 1371).

Chrysostom (Homilies on 1 Corinthians 40) took the verse to describe a rite of the Marcionites, which Paul uses as an argument against them. Marcion lived long after this letter, so that cannot be the practice Paul meant. Chrysostom also read the baptism as a confession of the resurrection of the dead. The Orthodox baptize each person once, and pray for the departed in memorial services.

Calvin on 15:29 says "for my part, however, I cannot by any means be persuaded" that the Corinthians were baptized at graves in place of the dead. He reads it as the baptism of those "looked upon as already dead," who "have altogether despaired of life," a custom he calls "sacred, and in accordance with the Divine institution." The later habit of putting off baptism until death he calls "a gross error."
Baptism is for those who profess faith personally (London Baptist Confession, chapter 29). The verse is read as a puzzling reference to a local custom, not as a command.
Baptism for the dead is a practice of the church, carried out in temples (Doctrine and Covenants 124:29-30), and 1 Corinthians 15:29 is read as describing it.

traditions.q: In what sense is the Son 'put under' the Father (15:24-28)?
views: The Son is equal to the Father in his divine nature and subject to him in his human nature, as Aquinas taught (Summa Theologiae III, question 20). The creed says "of his kingdom there will be no end"; the Son's handing over of the kingdom is the completion of his work.

The Formula of Concord (Solid Declaration 8:55 and 8:70) cites 1 Corinthians 15:27 among the texts showing that "all things in subjection beneath His feet" were given to the man Christ, together with all judgment and all power. It calls these "not created gifts, but divine, infinite properties," communicated to his assumed human nature.
Gregory of Nyssa read the verse as the subjection of humanity, Christ's body, to God, not of the divine Son, who is never less than the Father. The Nicene faith stands.

Calvin says Christ rules as "the Father's Vicegerent" without the Father being idle, since he "is of one essence with him, and is therefore himself God." Christ is "inferior to God" only "in respect of his human nature," and his being subjected means that, "the vail being then removed, we shall openly behold God reigning in his majesty." The Westminster Confession teaches that Christ's two whole natures, the Godhead and the manhood, are joined in one person, the only Mediator between God and man (8.2).

The study notes of the New World Translation (Watchtower Online Library) say that at 15:28 the Son will "subject himself to Jehovah's supreme sovereignty," humbly handing rulership back to his Father.

The Racovian Catechism (Polish Brethren, 1605; English translation by Thomas Rees, 1818) argues that Christ is not the supreme God. It cites 15:27, "it is manifest that He is excepted which did put all things under him," and 15:28, that "the Son himself would be subject unto him," as things "which could not have been predicated of Christ, had he possessed a divine nature."

The United Pentecostal Church International position paper "The True Humanity of Jesus Christ" (2004) does not discuss 15:24-28. It teaches that Christ's prayers, his "submission to the Father's will" and the Son's "lack of independent knowledge and power" arise from his humanity, that the titles "Father" and "Son" distinguish deity from humanity, and that taking them as two persons falls into "ditheism" or "subordinationism."

Some evangelicals (Wayne Grudem) hold that the Son eternally submits to the Father, a lasting difference of role within the Trinity with no difference of being, and read the Son's place under the Father here in that light. Others (Kevin Giles) criticize that teaching as a form of subordinationism.

traditions.q: What kind of body will be raised, and where are the dead until then?
views: The dead rise with their own bodies, changed and incorruptible; the soul, which is immortal, survives death and is judged at once, and may be purified before heaven (Catechism 988-1004, 1021-1022, 1030-1032).

The soul and body part at death and are reunited at the resurrection, when the body is raised in the likeness of Christ's risen body; the departed are remembered in the church's prayer (John of Damascus, Exact Exposition 4.27).
Christ will return and raise all the dead, to eternal life for the righteous and punishment for the wicked (Augsburg Confession, article 17).
At death the body returns to dust and the soul returns to God; on the last day the very same bodies, with different qualities, are raised and rejoined to their souls (Westminster Confession 32).
The righteous will have resurrected and glorified bodies and will live with the Lord forever (Baptist Faith and Message 2000, article 10).
Death is an unconscious state until the resurrection, when God gives the redeemed immortality (Fundamental Belief 26).

A Watchtower article, "The Two Resurrections" (15 November 1984), says Christ "was the first to be raised as a spirit person," quotes 15:42-44 for the change to spirit life, and calls the heavenly resurrection of the 144,000 the "first resurrection." It says a "second" resurrection of "both the righteous and the unrighteous" follows, with the chance of everlasting life on earth.
Every person will be resurrected with an immortal body of flesh and bones; the sun, moon and stars of 15:40-41 are taken as images of three kingdoms of glory (Doctrine and Covenants 76, 88, 130:22).

traditions.q: Does 'all will be made alive in Christ' mean every person will be saved?
views: Hell exists and is eternal (Catechism 1033-1037); the Church prays that all be saved but does not teach that they will be. Hans Urs von Balthasar argued that one may hope for it without claiming it.

The tradition is not unanimous. Origen and Gregory of Nyssa read 15:22-28 as God's final restoration of all: "all will be made alive" answers "all die in Adam," and "God all in all" leaves no one outside. The church later condemned Origen's teaching, and what Gregory taught is disputed among Orthodox and non-Orthodox scholars. Most Orthodox teach that hell is real while praying and hoping for all (Kallistos Ware argues that hope, not certainty, is allowed). David Bentley Hart, an Orthodox writer, argues for the universalist reading.
The Augsburg Confession (article 17) condemns those who teach that the punishment of the lost will end.
The second "all" means all who belong to Christ (15:23), and the Westminster Confession teaches that the last judgment brings "eternal salvation of the elect" and "damnation of the reprobate" (33.2).
The wicked will be condemned to eternal punishment and the righteous will have eternal life (Baptist Faith and Message 2000, article 10).

Most evangelicals teach eternal punishment for the lost. The philosopher Thomas Talbott, a Christian universalist, argues in The Inescapable Love of God that God will in the end save all; critics answer that the second "all" of 15:22 is limited by 15:23, "those who belong to Christ."

traditions.q: Does 15:51-52 describe a secret rapture before the tribulation?
views: The Dallas Theological Seminary Doctrinal Statement says the next event in prophecy is "the coming of the Lord in the air," and that "the translation of the church will be followed by the fulfillment of Israel's seventieth week," with the church in heaven during that time. The statement does not name 1 Corinthians 15:51-52.

Wikipedia lists George Ladd, John Piper, Robert Gundry and Douglas Moo among those who place the rapture at the end of the tribulation, and says it cites 1 Corinthians 15:51-52 there, for a trumpet that sounds at the end of the tribulation. It calls the mid-tribulation view a minority view among premillennialists, and describes a pre-wrath view that places the rapture during the tribulation, before the second coming. Ladd is also described as a proponent of historic premillennialism.
Christ will appear at the end of the world to judge, raising all the dead; the Augsburg Confession (article 17) speaks only of that one appearance of Christ and has no separate rapture.

The Nicene Creed, which the Orthodox Church confesses, says Christ "will come again, with glory, to judge the living and the dead." An Orthodox page on the Second Coming says "the emphasis of historic Orthodoxy is that Jesus will come again, not when He will come again," and lists pre-, post- and a-millennial camps and pre-, mid- and post-tribulation adherents among those divided. It does not mention a rapture.
The Church does not teach a rapture apart from the Lord's one return. The dead will rise at the last day and the living will be changed (Catechism 675-677, 1001).
There is one return of Christ, followed by the resurrection and the judgment; at the last day the living are changed and the dead raised (Westminster Confession 32.2 and 33.1).

title: Money, Plans and Greetings
sum: The last chapter turns from doctrine to business: a collection for the poor believers in Jerusalem, to be set aside each week (16:1-4), and Paul's travel plans. He will pass through Macedonia, perhaps winter at Corinth, and meanwhile stay at Ephesus until Pentecost because a great door has opened, even though many oppose him (16:5-9).

He sends Timothy, asks the Corinthians to treat him kindly, and reports that Apollos will come later (16:10-12). A few quick orders follow, including "Whatever you do should be done in love" (16:13-14). He praises Stephanas, Fortunatus and Achaicus, and the letter closes with greetings from Asia, Aquila and Prisca's house church, a holy kiss, Paul's own signature, a curse on those who do not love the Lord, the Aramaic prayer Marana tha, and his love for them all (16:15-24).
readings: On the usual reading these are the ordinary close of an ancient letter: travel plans, recommendations, greetings. They also show how Paul ran his mission, through a web of named people.
The last page as a summary of the letter

Another reading finds the themes of the letter in the ending: unity (a collection from all churches; Apollos and Paul on good terms), honor for servants not rich patrons (Stephanas), love (16:14, 24), and the Lord's coming (16:22). Some scholars read the whole letter as one appeal for unity, and these closing lines fit that.

views.H: The plan puts the letter in a spring at Ephesus (16:8). The collection for Jerusalem was begun in Galatia and Corinth and finished in Macedonia (2 Corinthians 8 and 9) and, with delegates from several provinces, taken to Jerusalem (Acts 20:4; 24:17). Corinth's visitors Stephanas, Fortunatus and Achaicus (Greek and Latin names) show how ordinary members of a Roman colony moved between cities. House churches such as Aquila and Prisca's met in large homes. The closing greetings, the signature in Paul's own hand and the blessing are in the manner of Greek letters, here made Christian.
views.C: Some partition theories treat 16:1-9 or 16:10-24 as belonging to another letter; most scholars hold that chapter 16 is the end of the letter we have. The Textus Receptus adds a postscript that says it was written from Philippi, which 16:8 contradicts. The sentence at 16:22 contains the one Aramaic phrase that Paul leaves untranslated in this letter, and 16:24, a final line of love, is without parallel in his other letters. The variants are at 16:19 (Prisca or Priscilla), 16:22 (two), 16:23 and 16:24.
views.L: The chapter returns to the themes of chapter 1: sending, receiving, honor. Paul repeats "firstfruits" (16:15, from 15:20, 23), and the closing sequence of greeting, kiss, signature, curse, prayer and blessing runs like a short liturgy. The command "Whatever you do should be done in love" (16:14) recalls chapter 13, and 16:24 returns to love to end.
views.J: The collection echoes the Temple tax Jews in the Diaspora sent each year to Jerusalem, and the prophets' picture of the nations bringing gifts to Zion (Isaiah 60:5-7); Paul pictures Gentile believers sending a gift to the mother church. "The first day of the week" is the Jewish way of naming Sunday. Pentecost is the Jewish festival of Weeks. The Aramaic prayer Marana tha probably comes from the Aramaic-speaking Jewish believers of Jerusalem (Antioch has also been proposed). A holy kiss was a custom of Jewish and Greek greeting alike.
views.T: The Didache uses Marana tha in the Lord's Supper prayers, and most churches have used the kiss of peace in their liturgy. Churches have used 16:2 for a weekly offering and Sunday worship; the cards below put them side by side.

deep.h: Why Paul cared about the collection
deep.b:
The collection ran through Paul's mission for years. At the meeting in Jerusalem he had agreed to "remember the poor" (Galatians 2:10). He raised money in Galatia, Corinth, Macedonia and Achaia (16:1; 2 Corinthians 8 and 9; Romans 15:26). When he wrote Romans he was about to deliver it and asked for prayer that it would be "acceptable" (Romans 15:30-31). Acts mentions it only in passing, in Paul's later defense, "I arrived to give alms for my people" (Acts 24:17). What happened when the money reached Jerusalem is not told.

Scholars give several purposes. Relief: the Jerusalem church was poor (Acts 11:28-30). Unity: a gift from Gentiles to Jews as a sign that the two groups were one body. Fulfilling prophecy: the nations bringing wealth to Zion (Isaiah 60:5-7), with Paul as the priest presenting the offering of the Gentiles (Romans 15:16). Obligation: Paul's Gentiles owed a debt to the Jews who gave them the gospel (Romans 15:27). Paul does not choose among them, and they are not exclusive.

He also set up safeguards: weekly saving so there is no pressure, delegates chosen by the churches and letters of introduction (16:2-3; 2 Corinthians 8:20-21).
deep.refs: Galatians 2:10; Romans 15:25; Romans 15:31; 2 Corinthians 8:1; Acts 11:28; Acts 20:4; Acts 24:17

deep.b: A handful of Aramaic words survived in the Greek-speaking churches: Abba (Romans 8:15; Galatians 4:6), amen, hosanna, Cephas (15:5), and Marana tha (16:22). Each shows how the first Aramaic-speaking Jewish believers prayed and spoke, and that the Gentile churches carried those words forward untranslated. "Our Lord, come" is a prayer addressed to Jesus using the word Mar, "Lord," a title that in Aramaic was used of God. Larry Hurtado holds that this shows devotion to Jesus appeared very early among Jewish believers, not late and among Gentiles. The Didache (10:6) and Revelation 22:20 both preserve the prayer, one in Aramaic and one in Greek.

deep.h: The first day of the week
deep.b: Paul does not call it "the Lord's day" and does not say that Christians meet. He says "on the first day of the week, each of you" should put something aside. Other early texts show that Christians met that day: Acts 20:7 at Troas; Revelation 1:10 ("the Lord's day"); the Didache 14:1; Ignatius of Antioch, who wrote that believers no longer keep Sabbaths but live by the Lord's day (Magnesians 9); and Justin Martyr (First Apology 67), who describes the Sunday gathering, the reading, the Eucharist and the offering for the needy. Jewish believers continued to keep the Sabbath for some time. The Council of Laodicea (about 363) told Christians not to rest on the Sabbath as Jews did but to honor the Lord's day.

echoes: Isaiah 60:5; Galatians 2:10; Romans 15:25; Romans 16:3; Romans 16:5; Acts 11:28; Acts 16:6; Acts 18:2; Acts 19:8; Acts 19:22; Acts 20:4; Acts 24:17; 2 Corinthians 1:15; 2 Corinthians 8; 2 Corinthians 9; Revelation 22:20; Didache 10:6; Didache 14:1

settings.to: The church at Corinth, as he had told the churches of Galatia
settings.when: in the spring before Pentecost, from Ephesus
settings.why: To set up a weekly saving so the gift for the poor in Jerusalem would be ready when he came and he would not need to ask under pressure. It also puts Corinth beside Galatia in one common project, a fund from the Gentile churches for the mother church. The Corinthians themselves had asked about it, since the opening words "Now about" probably reflect their letter (compare 7:1; 8:1; 12:1), though that use of the phrase is debated.
settings.readers: Roman-colony Corinthians, many with little money and used to the honor of patrons, now asked to give small, regular, private amounts that all could share.

settings.what: Travel plans and the sending of Timothy and Apollos
settings.why: To tell them when he will come and why he is staying, to protect Timothy from contempt, and to show that Paul and Apollos are friends, not rivals (compare 1:12; 3:4-6). It was also a way of taking the sting out of the "I belong to Paul" party.

settings.by: Paul, with the greeting in his own hand
settings.to: The church at Corinth, with greetings from the churches of Asia and from Aquila and Prisca's house church
settings.when: at the close of the letter, from Ephesus, in the spring, before Pentecost (16:8)
settings.why: To give a short rule of life (watch, stand, be brave, be strong, do all in love), to ask the church to honor workers like Stephanas, and to end with a holy kiss, a curse on those who do not love the Lord, the prayer Marana tha, and his own love. The last lines work as a liturgy that the assembly would hear aloud when the letter was read.

traditions.q: How much should Christians give, and is the tithe still binding?
views: The faithful have the duty of providing for the material needs of the Church, each according to his abilities (Catechism 2043), and giving alms to the poor is a work of justice pleasing to God (Catechism 2447).
The Heidelberg Catechism (1563, question 103) counts Christian alms among the duties of the day of worship. Reformed churches differ on whether the Old Testament tithe still binds.
Wesley's rule in his sermon on the use of money: gain all you can, save all you can, give all you can. It asks for no fixed share, only that the giving be as large as one can make it.
Christians should give cheerfully, regularly, systematically, proportionately and liberally (Baptist Faith and Message 2000, article 13); the language echoes 1 Corinthians 16:2.
The Hutterites hold goods in common, following Acts 2 and 4, so that no one is in need (Peter Rideman, Account of Our Religion, 1540); other Anabaptist groups practice mutual aid.
Faithful stewardship includes returning a tithe and giving offerings to support the church's mission (Fundamental Belief 21).
Tithing, one tenth of one's income, is a command for members, based on the revelation in Doctrine and Covenants 119.

traditions.q: Which day is the Christian day of worship (16:2)?
views: Sunday, the Lord's Day, replaces the Sabbath as the day of worship and rest, because Christ rose on it (Catechism 2174-2176).
The Council of Laodicea (about 363, canon 29) told Christians not to rest on the Sabbath like the Jews but to honor the Lord's day, and to rest then if they could.
The Sabbath law is no longer bound to a day; Sunday is kept because the church needs a regular time for the word and sacrament (Luther, Large Catechism, on the third commandment).
The Sabbath command remains in force and was moved to the first day, which is to be kept holy (Westminster Confession 21.7-8).
The seventh-day Sabbath still binds all (Fundamental Belief 20); 16:2 speaks of saving at home for a collection and does not make Sunday a holy day.
The Lord's Day is a Christian institution kept for worship and rest in memory of the resurrection (Baptist Faith and Message 2000, article 8).
